summary:
Sabah is assessed under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping; the offence is not limited to Malaysian citizens and applies to foreign visitors. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, additionally records that transgender people can be targeted through the "gross indecency" offence as well as through state Sharia enactments prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females".

Like every other Malaysian state, Sabah maintains a Sharia enactment of this kind. These state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them, whereas the federal Penal Code reaches everyone present in the territory.

Enforcement is reported as active. The Human Dignity Trust profile records arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under the federal and state layers since the 2018 election, and Human Rights Watch, in a report with Justice for Sisters published on 10 August 2022, documents a crackdown that has persisted since that election through arrests and criminal proceedings at both the federal and the state-Sharia level.

The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows the machinery a transgender person can face: a transgender woman was pursued on a religious-affairs arrest warrant, with a search mobilising 122 officers. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters call for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity in response to the pattern they document.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the practical exposure is the federal Penal Code rather than Sharia, and the documented pattern of enforcement is arrest and prosecution rather than private-conduct policing alone.
tangentialFactors:
The federal penalty ceiling of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping is among the highest in the region for consensual same-sex conduct, and the state Sharia layer adds up to three years' imprisonment, a fine and caning for cross-dressing where it applies to Muslims.

The Nur Sajat matter indicates the scale of resources state religious authorities will commit against a single transgender individual: an arrest warrant for offending religious sensitivities and a 122-officer search, before the case drew international attention.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters place Malaysia among the countries where LGBT people face state-backed discrimination rather than isolated private prejudice, and their 10 August 2022 report presses for decriminalisation as the remedy, a reform for which no legislative movement is documented in these sources.

The Human Dignity Trust profile is a national-level document and is periodically updated; its enforcement findings since the 2018 election are drawn from country-wide reporting rather than from any single state.
localsOnly:
Malaysian citizens and residents face both layers at once. The federal Penal Code offences apply irrespective of consent, and the state Sharia cross-dressing provisions apply to Muslims, enforced by the state Islamic religious department under Sabah's own enactment.

The Sharia laws criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman" do not define what constitutes transgender dress, leaving the boundary to the enforcing officers; penalties under such enactments nationally reach three years' imprisonment, a fine and caning.

Since the 2018 election, arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment have been documented at both the federal and state-Sharia levels, so residents who are visibly gender-nonconforming carry exposure in everyday public space, not only at venues subject to raids.

Transgender Malaysians have used litigation and advocacy to resist the regime: Justice for Sisters works alongside Human Rights Watch on documentation and reform demands, and the Nur Sajat case became a focal point for criticism of religious-affairs enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither the Human Dignity Trust profile (updated 16 December 2025) nor the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report (10 August 2022) contains Sabah-specific findings; both are national-level documents. Sabah-specific arrest, prosecution or raid figures are therefore not sourced here and remain unresolved.

The precise text, penalties and enforcement record of Sabah's own Sharia enactment are not sourced in this inventory; the state-level description given here rests on the national pattern of such enactments.

Whether Sabah's enactment also bars women from posing as men, as some other Malaysian states do, is not sourced here.

No entry, visa, document-marker or facility rules specific to Sabah are covered by these sources; the assessment rests on criminal-law and enforcement material only.
